summary: Defines two formats and media types for representing sets of links as standalone documents: one based on JSON and one aligned with the HTTP Link header field format. It also introduces a link relation type for discovering such link sets. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A web page can carry many connections to other things. Instead of squeezing them all into small labels, this lets them be written in one separate list, which others can find and read.

questions: how to publish a set of links as json
what is the linkset link relation type

subtitle: Two standalone document formats and a link relation type for publishing a whole set of web links in one place.

tldr.problem: Web links normally travel in the HTTP Link header or inside a page, but sometimes that is impractical or impossible: the links may come from another party, be hard to write into headers, or be too many to fit predictably.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines application/linkset, which is almost the same as the Link header field value, and application/linkset+json, a JSON form of the same model. It also defines the linkset link relation type so that a resource can point to its link set.
tldr.outcome: Links can be delivered as a separate, self-contained document and discovered with a typed link. Both formats can round trip with the Link header, as long as JSON extensions stay limited.

today: RFC 9264 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on RFC 8288 for the Web Linking model.

sections.title: Why Link Sets Exist
sections.content:
Resources on the Web often use typed Web Links (RFC 8288), either embedded in the representation, as with the HTML <link> element, or conveyed in the HTTP Link header field. Sometimes providing links that way is impractical or impossible, and a standalone document is better.

RFC 9264 defines two formats for sets of Web Links and their attributes. One serializes links in the same format as the Link header field. The other uses JSON. It also defines media types for them and the linkset relation type for discovering a resource that carries a link set.
sections.eli5: Sometimes there are too many labels to tie onto a package. So you write them all on one sheet instead.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC gives three situations where a standalone link document helps.

  • Third-party links. A server other than the one hosting a resource can provide links about it, including links where the resource is the target rather than the context, or links managed by a special-purpose link service.
  • Hard to write headers. An application may lack some of the needed link information or the ability to write HTTP fields directly.
  • Many links. The size of a Link header can become unpredictable when links are computed dynamically. A server can be configured with an upper bound, but estimating one is hard, and no error code says that a field was truncated. A standalone document avoids the problem.

Other mechanisms can still be combined with a link set.
sections.eli5: A friend can write down links about your page, or you may have too many to squeeze into a label, so a separate list is easier.

sections.title: The application/linkset Format
sections.content:
Both formats follow the model of RFC 8288: each link has a link context, a link relation type, a link target and optional target attributes. The application/linkset format is nearly identical to a Link header field value. The difference is that newline characters are also allowed as separators, to help humans read it. Non-ASCII characters are not allowed. When converting to a Link header, newlines MUST be removed or replaced by whitespace.

It differs from application/link-format of RFC 6690, which adds constraints for constrained environments.

Link sets can be reused outside an HTTP exchange, so the RFC recommends making them self-contained: give every link an explicit anchor, use URI references that are not relative, and use title* rather than title so the language travels with the title. The deprecated rev construct is not carried; inverse links are expressed by switching the roles of the resources.
sections.eli5: It looks like the usual link label, but you may break it into several lines so people can read it.

sections.title: The JSON Format
sections.content:
The application/linkset+json format MUST be encoded as UTF-8. A link set is a JSON object whose sole member is linkset, an array of link context objects. Even a single object MUST be wrapped in an array.

Each link context object may have an anchor member holding the link context, which MUST be a URI reference and SHOULD NOT be relative. For each relation type it adds one member whose name is the registered relation name or, for extension types, the URI. Its value is an array of link target objects, which MUST be an array even for a single target.

Each link target object MUST have an href with the target URI reference. If the target is the resource that provides the link set, the value is an empty string. Other members carry target attributes.

JSON-LD is optionally supported by adding a context, and Appendix A shows one that lets the JSON be read as RDF data.
sections.eli5: It is a list of boxes. Each box says 'from here', then a kind of connection, then the places it connects to.

sections.title: Target Attributes and Extensions
sections.content:
The attributes defined by RFC 8288 are hreflang, media, title, title* and type. In JSON they are members of the link target object. hreflang is repeatable, so its value MUST be an array of strings.

Internationalized attributes follow RFC 8187 and end in an asterisk, like title*. In JSON the value is an array of objects with a value member holding the unescaped content and an optional language member with the language tag. Encoding information is not preserved, and tools MUST decode and encode correctly when converting between the two formats.

Extension attributes defined by communities are always treated as repeatable, so their values MUST be arrays. Other kinds of JSON extension are NOT RECOMMENDED, because limiting the format allows unambiguous round trips between the Link header, the text format and the JSON format. If extensions are used, they MUST NOT change the meaning of the defined members, and consumers can ignore them.
sections.eli5: Each connection can carry extra notes such as language or type. Extra private notes are allowed, as long as they do not change the meaning of the normal ones.

sections.title: Discovery and Profiles
sections.content:
The target of a link with the linkset relation type provides a set of links, including links in which the linking resource participates. The link can appear in a header field or in a body, and a resource MAY have more than one, for example to the same set in different media types or to sets from different third parties.

The linked set may contain links for which the linking resource is not the context. User agents MUST process each link independently and MAY ignore links in which the context of the linkset link does not participate. If anchors or targets are relative, a user agent MUST determine the context and SHOULD ignore a link it cannot determine unambiguously.

The optional profile parameter of the two media types, and a profile attribute on a linkset link, name one or more space-separated URIs identifying constraints or conventions, for example a limited set of relation types. A profile does not change the semantics of the link set, so clients that do not know it can use the same representation. Examples in the RFC show a GET returning each format and a HEAD response whose Link header points at a link set.
sections.eli5: A note on the package says where the list is. A sticker can also say which rulebook the list follows, but you can read the list without it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
RFC 9264 registers one link relation type, linkset, in the Link Relation Types registry, and two media types in the Media Types registry: application/linkset and application/linkset+json. Both media types have profile as an optional parameter and no required parameters. The change controller is the IETF.

For application/linkset+json, the encoding and interoperability considerations of RFC 8259 apply. For the JSON type, the RFC says it does not propose a specific file extension other than the generic .json.
sections.eli5: The names of the two list formats and the 'list is here' connection were put in an official phone book so everyone uses them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of Section 7 of RFC 3986 apply, as do those of RFC 8288, except where those discuss exposing information in HTTP header fields. Links can leak information such as URIs that are sensitive or private, so URIs exposed in links should not be 'hidden' ones. Resources meant for limited users should have technical protection.

Two issues are specific to link sets. First, the implicit context of a Web Link is the resource of the HTTP exchange, and it can be lost or change when self-contained link representations are moved. Applications may ignore links without an explicit anchor, or with relative URIs, when exchanged as standalone resources.

Second, third-party links let one party provide links anchored on another party's resource. Applications should verify there is enough trust in that party and may treat third-party links differently.
sections.eli5: A list of links can accidentally show secret addresses. And if someone else wrote the list, you should check you trust them.
